3.0.s.en: 1. Obedience is the way to favor in the sight of God and man

3.0.0.en: 1 My son, forget not my law; but let your heart keep my commandments: 2 For length of days, and long life, and peace, shall they add to you. 3 Let not mercy and truth forsake you: bind them about your neck; write them upon the table of your heart: 4 So shall you find favor and good understanding in the sight of God and man.

3.0.1.en: “My son, forget not my law; but let your heart keep my commandments.

3.0.2.en: For length of days, and long life, and peace, shall they add to you” [1].

3.0.3.en: The wise Solomon begins by revealing obedience as the way of wisdom. Perhaps the speaker here is Solomon as a spiritual father and guide, or the speaker is “Wisdom,” that is, “the Lord Christ.” In any case, obedience is a participation with the Lord Christ in His nature: “[He] became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Phil 2:8). As we abide in Him as members of His body, we bear the spirit of obedience to God, to His commandment, to His servants, and to those who lead us in the Lord. We even find sweetness in practicing obedience toward those who are younger than we are or less than we are in knowledge, so long as it is “in the Lord.” St. Pachomius wept and mourned for a time in repentance because he had not obeyed the words of his spiritual son Theodore. The latter was responsible for the clothing store and asked his father to exchange his worn-out garment for a new one, but the father refused... Yet he regretted his disobedience to his son!

3.0.4.en: In brief, Solomon calls his disciple with a tender fatherly spirit, asking him to remember the law of his spiritual father, indeed the law of the Lord which his father speaks. He should repeat it constantly in his depths and on his tongue so that he does not forget it, and he should practice what he remembers so that it may be kept all the more within the heart. It is as though he says to him: “I do not ask only that you remember it in your mind and keep it by heart, but what is more important is that you engrave it on your heart and practice it. In this way the commandment enters the heart, not so that the heart may lock it up like a precious jewel that must merely be hidden away, but so that it may reign over the heart and lead it in the royal way, and bring it into the very bosom of God.” Thus the heart acquires the “wisdom of God,” the Lord Christ, the Giver of all treasures and riches, bearing a share in the nature of His sweet obedience.

3.0.5.en: In the Midnight Prayer we repeat what the prophet David says: “Your word I have hidden in my heart, that I might not sin against You” (Ps 119:11). We also continually repeat what was said of the young priest Ezra: “For Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the Lord, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments” (Ezra 7:10).

3.0.6.en: When we hear: “For length of days, and long life, and peace, shall they add to you” [1], we do not desire to remain on the face of the earth, even though that is a good divine gift, but we ask for the lengthening of our fruitful days. Many remained alive even after their death; their life story, their prayers and their words remained at work in the lives of people. Though they died, they work through the grace of God that was given to them.

3.0.7.en: The wise man says, “years of life,” because some live “years of death.” Perhaps the days of their sojourn on earth extend to tens of years, but they are years of death, bearing neither life nor love; their presence on earth is like their absence...

3.0.8.en: As for peace, the believer asks for the “peace” of the inner heart, even if fire surrounds him on every side, so that he practices, with the three young men, their praise while in the furnace of fire.

3.0.9.en: By obedience in the Lord, springing from the heart, we walk the royal way, the way of mercy and truth.

3.1.0.en: “Let not mercy and truth forsake you: bind them about your neck” [3].

3.1.1.en: By saying, “forsake you not,” it is clear that he is not speaking of two mere characteristics, but of a personal relationship with mercy and truth, who here in reality are the divine Hypostasis of the Word, who desires neither to leave us nor to be left by us.

3.1.2.en: Our Christ is the Way. When we acquire Him, we bear the spirit of love, mercy and kindness, this Spirit who walks in the truth without deviating to the right or to the left. In our love we bear the truth, and in our holding fast to the truth we practice love. For love without truth turns into a looseness that kills the soul as well as others, and truth without love begets anger that corrupts the eyes. True love is the other side of truth, and true truth is the other face of love!

3.1.3.en: When we practice mercy and truth, the commandments that seem exceedingly heavy, and at times impossible, turn into a precious and beautiful necklace with which the neck of the soul is adorned as a heavenly princess, as happened with Joseph in the house of Potiphar (Gen 41:41). Therefore he says: “bind them about your neck” [3].

3.1.4.en: The two commandments of mercy and truth enter into the depths, and there they are engraved on the two tablets of the heart, so that events cannot incline the believer to one side or the other, but he walks uprightly. Therefore it is said: “write them upon the table of your heart” [3].

3.1.5.en: St. John Chrysostom comments on the saying, “Let not mercy and truth forsake you” [3], saying that our relationship with God and His commandments is not a temporary relationship for a short period, but that we hold fast to mercy and truth continually without interruption and never leave them, so that they do not leave us, for we need them at all times.

3.1.6.en: * It is fitting for us to please God not once, but continually. He who enters a race, if he runs ten laps and stops running the last distance, loses all that he has done. So we too, if we begin good works and then become negligent, lose all that we have done and spoil everything.

3.1.7.en: Listen to the profitable counsel: “Let not mercy and truth forsake you” [3]. He does not say, do this once, or twice, or three times, or ten or a hundred times, but “let them not forsake you,” showing that we are the ones who need them, and not they who need us. He teaches us that we must exert all effort to keep them with us.

3.1.8.en: * Let us obey them now, not for one day, nor for three days, but the wise man says: “Let not mercy and truth forsake you.” He did not say: “once or twice.” As we know, the virgins had oil that remained with them to the end (Mt 25:3, 8). So we too need much oil, that we may be like the green olive tree in the house of the Lord (Ps 52:8).

3.1.9.en: St. John Chrysostom — The two commandments of mercy and truth are placed around the neck so that they may be the object of our sight and we never ignore them, and they are engraved on the tablet of the heart so that they may absorb all our feelings and reign over our senses; we feel them with our hearts as we see them with our inner eyes.

3.2.0.en: The fruit of obedience, which brings us into this way, is: “So shall you find favor and good understanding in the sight of God and man” [4]. God is pleased with us and grants us holy understanding more and more, and although some oppose us, many honor us and seek our counsel.

3.2.1.en: Thus the wise man urges us to strive, by the grace of God, to cling to mercy and truth continually until we reach perfection. In the discourse of the blessed Clement on virginity, he spoke of the necessity of ceaseless, continual striving to attain perfect virtue, and that virgins should not stop at the outward appearance of virginity.

3.2.2.en: * It is fitting for all virgins of both sexes who have truly resolved to keep virginity for the sake of the Kingdom of Heaven, each one of them, to be qualified for the Kingdom of God in everything. For it is not by eloquence, nor by fame, nor by position, nor by origin, nor by beauty or strength, nor by length of life that we reach the Kingdom of Heaven, but we obtain it by the power of faith, when a man shows the works of faith. For whoever is truly righteous, his works bear witness to his faith; he truly believes, with great faith, perfect faith, faith in God, a faith that shines in good works, so that the Father of all is glorified in Christ.

3.2.3.en: Now those who are truly virgins for the sake of God submit to the One who says: “Let not mercy and truth forsake you: bind them about your neck. So shall you find favor and good understanding in the sight of God and man” [3, 4].

3.2.4.en: St. Clement of Rome — Finally, by saying, “Let not mercy and truth forsake you,” he calls us to be in their constant company, for they are two faithful friends whose continual companionship we need. Rather, they are one Friend, the Person of the Lord Christ, “the Mercy and the Truth,” to whom we hold fast, saying with the bride who strove to seek Him, found Him, and held Him and would not let Him go (Song 3:4). She clung to Him as to her own Bridegroom alone, saying to those around her: “I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that you stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please” (Song 3:5).

3.3.s.en: 2. Trust in God makes straight the paths of man

3.3.0.en: “Trust in the Lord with all your heart; and lean not unto your own understanding.

3.3.1.en: In all your ways acknowledge Him, and He shall direct your paths” [5, 6].

3.3.2.en: These are the most important commandments, connected with our faith in God, the Source of all good things, the Lover of mankind, the almighty and wise heavenly Father who cares for us even in small matters, who promises and fulfills His promise to us. It is fitting for us to trust in the Lord with all our hearts, for He wishes to give us what is best and is able to do so. Those who know themselves realize that their understanding, without divine help, is like a broken reed: if they lean on it, they fail. Therefore it is fitting that we plan nothing except what is in harmony with the divine commandment, asking God for His counsel, as we ask Him to sanctify our thought and lead our conduct. Truly, whoever relies on his understanding, his experience and his abilities without divine help is foolish!

3.3.3.en: In all our ways, whether private, family, or related to work or the society around us, it is fitting that we acknowledge God as our Leader, so that we submit to Him and declare our joy in fulfilling His will and commandments. Then He directs our ways and makes them straight, and we live in peace and happiness, rightly dividing His word in our lives (1 Tim 2:15).

3.3.4.en: We acknowledge Him as our Leader at the beginning of every way we walk, accompanying us throughout our journey, speaking with us and we with Him without interruption, and bringing us across to the end. Then we say with the two disciples of Emmaus: “Did not our heart burn within us, while He talked with us by the way, and while He opened to us the scriptures?” (Lk 24:22).

3.4.s.en: 3. Humility grants healing to soul and body

3.4.0.en: 7 Be not wise in your own eyes: fear the Lord, and depart from evil. 8 It shall be health to your navel, and marrow to your bones.

3.4.1.en: We cannot practice obedience, nor enjoy trust in the Lord, by any way other than humility. Therefore he says:

3.4.2.en: “Be not wise in your own eyes.

3.4.3.en: Fear the Lord, and depart from evil. It shall be health to your navel, and marrow to your bones” [7, 8].

3.4.4.en: The wisdom that God gives us grants not only healing to the soul alone, but also offers a special blessing to the body, so that a person enjoys healing for his navel, that is, for the hidden sicknesses of his belly, and it becomes a hidden marrow within his bones, that is, for the frame of his body, or for his bodily strength. When we honor the Lord with a spirit of humility, He comes to us as a Physician for our souls and bodies, working in our hidden depths to give us life, growth and strength.

3.4.5.en: The wise man points to the healing of the navel because the believer regards himself as an embryo in the womb of the Church his mother, whose spiritual growth is not yet complete. He does not receive food by his mouth or by any other organ, but enjoys life and growth through the umbilical cord, which reveals God’s work with him through the Church. Without this divine work the embryo dies and is not born. So without divine wisdom the soul dies and has no existence in the heavenly places.

3.5.0.en: “Honor the Lord with your substance, and with the firstfruits of all your increase: so shall your barns be filled with plenty, and your presses shall burst out with new wine.” [9, 10].

3.5.1.en: In the Old Testament the believers offered the firstfruits, that is, the firstborn of the flocks and the firstfruits of the crops at harvest time. They offered them in the temple of God on the day of Pentecost (Num 28:26). By this they declared their longing to offer to God everything they possess, honoring the Lord with all their hearts and from their possessions, their works and their money. He declared to His people that the whole earth is His, and for this reason the commandment came confirming that they should not sell the land forever, for it belongs to God (Lev 25:23). So the believer feels that he has received the land of his heart from the hands of God, as the people of Israel received the land of Canaan. We are not content to offer God the chief place in the heart, but we hand the whole heart over to Him, to receive it anew from His hands as faithful stewards of what is His!

3.5.2.en: The New Testament warns us against expecting God to reward us with material blessings in return for our godliness (1 Tim 6:3-6). For God does not want to hire Christians, since He does not want them to be hired servants, but sons of His, in the likeness of the Lord Christ, in love, holiness and purity. He wants us to seek Him for His own sake, not that He may give us bodily or material gain. The reward of obedience to God is clinging to Him, enjoying a deeper union with Him, and His dwelling within us (Jn 14:15-18, 21-31). He also wants us to be content with what He supplies to us and not to covet what is more (1 Tim 6:6).

3.6.s.en: 5. Accepting the Lord’s chastening is a practical exercise of sonship

3.6.0.en: “My son, despise not the chastening of the Lord; neither be weary of His correction: for whom the Lord loves He corrects; even as a father the son in whom he delights.” [11-12].

3.6.1.en: The Apostle Paul quoted this passage in his Epistle to the Hebrews to link the Lord’s chastening with sonship to Him, saying: “And ye have forgotten the exhortation which speaketh unto you as unto children, My son, despise not the chastening of the Lord, nor faint when you are rebuked of Him: for whom the Lord loves He chastens, and scourges every son whom He receives. But if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers (that is, in chastisement), then are ye bastards, and not sons” (Heb 12:5-8).

3.6.2.en: The Apostle presents the following truths: 1. The believer receives every affliction as chastening from the Lord and not from men, for God chastens out of His nature as “God is love,” confirming His nature that radiates love upon us however severe the chastening may seem. Any chastening, even if it comes from a tender heart, is counted severe when compared with divine chastening. The Lord chastens according to what He sees for our edification and as much as we can bear! 2. If we receive chastening without thanksgiving, it turns into a bitter rebuke and we faint. It is as though what befalls us of troubles depends on our view of divine chastening: the view that springs from a filial heart sees edification in chastening, and his soul rejoices, while the grumbler sees in it a bitter rebuke. 3. All sons are partakers in chastening... without it a man is an illegitimate son (one of the bastards)!

3.6.3.en: God in His fatherly love sometimes visits us with afflictions and sicknesses for our edification, to make us wise and good. As for us, since we realize our sonship to Him, we do not collapse before trials, however heavy they are or however long they last. We never despair and never sin, but we wait for the salvation of the Lord with thanksgiving.

3.6.4.en: God does not scourge the sons of Satan; He strikes His own sons. For the coming of chastenings is a good witness that you belong to Him, as Eliphaz the Temanite says in his speech with Job during his trial: “Behold, happy is the man whom God corrects: therefore despise not the chastening of the Almighty: for He makes sore, and binds up: He wounds, and His hands make whole. He shall deliver you in six troubles: yes, in seven there shall no evil touch you” (Job 5:17-19).

3.6.5.en: * The words: “My son, depart not from the chastening of the Lord” are addressed to the free will of man. The Lord said: “I have prayed for you, that your faith fail not” (Lk 22:32), so that man may lean on grace.

3.6.6.en: St. Augustine — * He teaches us to give thanks and rejoice more and more when we are counted worthy of chastening. He says: “Whom I love I chasten.” How blessed a servant you are, since the Lord cares to correct you! He condescends and is angry with you! He does not deceive you by hiding His rebukes!

3.6.7.en: In all cases we must bind ourselves to the duty of patience, whether the trials come because of our faults, or proceed from the snares of the enemy, or are rebukes from the Lord. For the reward of this duty (patience) is great, namely happiness. For who is it that the Lord calls happy but the patient one, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

3.7.0.en: Tertullian, the scholar — * Thus the chastening of wisdom (“for whom the Lord loves He corrects” [12]) causes pains in order to bring understanding and to restore peace and immortality.

3.7.1.en: St. Clement of Alexandria — * If God rebukes the one He loves, and rebukes him with the aim of correcting him, so the brethren, especially the priests, do not hate those they rebuke but love them, for the sake of their correction. For God also foretold through Jeremiah, pointing to our own time, saying: “And I will give you pastors according to My heart, which shall feed you with the food of chastening” (Jer 3:15).

3.7.2.en: St. Cyprian — * Rebuke is bringing sin forward and setting it before the person. This kind of teaching is necessary in the highest degree, because of the weakness of faith of many... God uses the language of pain and blows that belongs to rebuke while offering His consolations through Solomon, hinting in a hidden way at His love toward the sons who respond to His teaching. “My son, despise not the chastening of the Lord...” “A sinful man will flee from reproof” (Sir 32:21). Therefore the Scripture says: “Let the righteous correct me and reprove me, but let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head.”

3.7.3.en: St. Clement of Alexandria — * Hear the words of David: “It is good for me that I have been afflicted, that I might learn Your statutes” (Ps 119:71). And another prophet says: “It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth” (Lam 3:27). And again: “Blessed is the man whom You chasten, O Lord” (Ps 94:12). And another says: “Despise not the chastening of the Lord” (Prov 3:11). And again: “If you come forward to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation” (Sir 11:1). As the Lord Christ also said to His disciples: “In the world you shall have tribulation, but rejoice” (Jn 16:33).

3.7.4.en: And again: “You shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy” (Jn 16:20). And again: “How narrow is the gate” (Mt 7:14). Do you see how affliction is praised everywhere?!

3.7.5.en: St. John Chrysostom — * Let the sick be advised that they realize they are sons of God when they are scourged with the whips of chastening. For if God did not aim to give them an inheritance after their correction, He would not care to instruct them by sorrows. Therefore the Lord says to John through the angel: “As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten” (Rev 3:19; Prov 3:11). It is also written: “My son, despise not the chastening of the Lord, nor faint when you are rebuked of Him: for whom the Lord loves He chastens, and scourges every son whom He receives” (Heb 12:5, 6). The psalmist says: “Many are the afflictions of the righteous: but the Lord delivers him out of them all” (Ps 33:20). Likewise blessed Job cries out in his grief and says: “If I am justified, I will not lift up my head, for I am full of dishonor and beholding my humiliation” (Job 10:15).

3.7.6.en: Let the sick be told that if they believe the heavenly city to be their city, they need to endure labors in this city as those who are in a foreign land. For if stones must be struck with the axe outside so that they may be set in the building of the temple of the Lord without the sound of the axe, so also we are now struck with whips from without so that afterwards we may be set in inner places, without the blows of chastening, in the temple of God.

3.7.7.en: In the end these blows remove what is unprofitable and unnecessary, and through the unity of love alone we are joined together in the building.

3.7.9.en: * Now God punishes in anger the sons of wrath, but He punishes (chastens) in mercy the sons of grace.

3.8.s.en: 6. Seeking wisdom is the way of blessedness, wealth and glory

3.8.0.en: 13 Blessed is the man who finds wisdom, and the man who gets understanding. 14 For the merchandise of it is better than the merchandise of silver, and the gain thereof than fine gold. 15 She is more precious than pearls, and all your jewels cannot equal her. 16 Length of days is in her right hand; and in her left hand riches and glory. 17 Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace. 18 She is a tree of life to those who lay hold upon her, and blessed is the one who holds her fast. 19 The Lord by wisdom has founded the earth; by understanding has He established the heavens. 20 By His knowledge the depths are broken up, and the clouds drop down the dew.

3.8.1.en: “Blessed is the man who finds wisdom, and the man who finds understanding” [13].

3.8.2.en: It is fitting for the believer to seek wisdom, to labor in searching for her, and to ask the Lord to acquire her, for she grants the blessed life, and offers him true and lasting riches and glory.

3.8.3.en: He says “blessed”... because the enjoyment of wisdom makes us partake of union with the Father in His Son by the Holy Spirit. This new life is a participation in the divine life, which is worthy of being called blessed. The Lord Christ opened His Sermon on the Mount with the call to enjoy this blessed life, repeating the word “blessed...” (Mt 5). For God created us to experience this blessed life, which we receive in its full form in the life to come.

3.8.4.en: The wise man sees that the earnest search for wisdom is like a business or a serious venture which the believer undertakes in order to gain profit. Believers are investors looking for spiritual gains.

3.8.5.en: The wise man compares wisdom and the gains she brings with worldly ventures and the wealth they bring, affirming that precious jewels and the treasures of the earth cannot be compared with true divine wisdom. The former are temporal and passing, while the latter is eternal. The former is the enjoyment of some gifts, while the latter is the possession of the Giver of gifts and Creator of all. Truly blessed is he who finds the Lord Christ, who is Wisdom, leading us by His Holy Spirit in our daily life.

3.8.6.en: “For the merchandise of it is better than the merchandise of silver, and the gain thereof than fine gold”

3.9.0.en: She is more precious than pearls, and all your jewels cannot equal her” [14-15].

3.9.1.en: This very phrase is among many phrases through which spiritual investors exercise their right of choice; from this we exercise this right as free people, relying on the riches of God’s grace.

3.9.2.en: “Take my instruction, and not silver; and knowledge rather than choice gold. Wisdom is better than pearls, and all the jewels cannot equal her” (Prov 8:11).

3.9.3.en: “Better is little with the fear of the Lord than great treasure with disgrace. Better is a meal of herbs where love is than a fatted ox and with it, silver” (Prov 15:16, 17).

3.9.4.en: “My fruit (the fruit of wisdom) is better than gold, yes, than fine gold; and my revenue than choice silver” (Prov 8:19).

3.9.5.en: “Better it is to be of a humble spirit with the lowly, than to divide the spoil with the proud” (Prov 16:19).

3.9.6.en: “He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that rules his spirit than he that takes a city” (Prov 16:32).

3.9.7.en: “Better is a dry morsel, and peace with it, than a house full of sacrifices with strife” (Prov 17:1).

3.9.8.en: “Better is the poor that walks in his integrity than he that is perverse in his lips, and is a fool” (Prov 19:1).

3.9.9.en: “A good name is better than great riches, and good favor better than silver and gold” (Prov 22:1).

3.9.10.en: “Open rebuke is better than secret love” (Prov 27:5).

3.9.11.en: * Wisdom proclaims: “Blessed is the man who finds wisdom, and the mortal who sees understanding, for from her goes forth righteousness, and her tongue carries law and mercy” [13, 16 LXX]. For the Law and the Gospel are both the work of the one Lord, who is mercy, because in Him is our salvation.

3.9.12.en: St. Clement of Alexandria — The psalmist says: “The law of Your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold and silver” (Ps 119:72). And St. John Chrysostom asks: Was St. Peter poor when he had neither gold nor silver to give to the lame man?

3.9.13.en: * This means: better for me is the Law that proceeds from Your mouth, which is Christ. I despise the shining pieces of gold and silver so that I may delight in the law of Your mouth and enjoy it.

3.9.14.en: We can say that the “law of the mouth” is the order of the words that come from the mouth of God: the first words were spoken to beginners, while the following words were spoken to those who had received the first, until they reach perfection.

3.9.15.en: Origen, the scholar — * The prophet says that for him the law of the mouth of God is better than all the desires of the world, referring to the desires by the shining pieces of gold and silver.

3.9.16.en: St. Augustine — * By the allegorical interpretation, silver represents the intellect, and gold indicates the spirit. So although there are thousands of pieces of gold and silver which those who dispute with the wisdom of the world use in the schools of philosophy, yet he who lives the divine wisdom and divine truth says: “The law of the mouth of the Lord is better for me.” Truly, only the Law that proceeds from the mouth of God can offer true gain to those who hold fast to it.

3.9.17.en: St. Didymus the Blind — Thousands of gold or silver may be lost or stolen or endanger the life of their owner, but the law of the mouth of the Lord offers a riches that is firm forever, which no one can take away from us.

3.9.18.en: St. Clement of Alexandria uses the previous phrase [13] in directing women who busy themselves with piercing their ears to put very costly “earrings” in them, and with putting special cosmetics for adorning the eyes, explaining that the ear’s listening to the voice of wisdom is natural and more precious than all jewels, and that the opening of the eyes to see divine and holy things is true beauty, where the believer sees what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man.

3.9.19.en: * Do not let your ears be pierced contrary to nature, so that “earrings” may be attached to them and hang from them. For it is not fitting to compel nature to do what is contrary to it. And there can be no ornament that adorns the ear better than the teaching that finds a natural path in the passages of hearing.

3.9.20.en: The anointing of the eyes with the Word and the piercing of the ears with the commandment make a man a listener and a contemplator of divine and holy things, and the Word declares true beauty: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard” (1 Cor 2:9).

3.10.0.en: St. Clement of Alexandria — “Length of days is in her right hand; and in her left hand riches and glory; out of her mouth proceeds righteousness, and her tongue carries law and mercy” (Septuagint) [16].

3.10.1.en: * The adornment of her right hand is the extension of generations, where the Word says: “Length of days is in her right hand.”

3.10.2.en: And in her left hand is the wealth of precious virtues with the splendor of glory: “in her left hand riches and glory” [16].

3.10.3.en: Solomon then speaks of the fragrance of the bride’s mouth, which gives off the good fragrance of righteousness:

3.10.5.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa — Some of the Fathers see that the right hand here refers to the eternal good things and glories, while the left hand refers to temporal blessings on earth. Therefore the bride sings in the Song, saying: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me” (Song 2:6). This is the living voice of the Church, which seeks the eternal glories as a right hand that embraces her, but is not much occupied with temporal blessings.

3.10.6.en: * The Church says in the voice of the elect: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me” (Song 2:6).

3.10.7.en: The left hand of God means the abundant good things in the present life, which the Church places under her head to press upon them because of her exalted love.

3.10.8.en: But the right hand of God embraces her, for in her complete consecration she is enveloped with eternal blessings. Therefore Solomon says again that length of days (eternity) is in her right hand, while in her left hand are riches and glory [16].

3.10.9.en: By speaking of riches and glory as placed in her left hand, he showed in what manner we look to them. Therefore the psalmist says: “Save me by Your right hand” (Ps 17:7). For he did not say “by Your hand,” but “by Your right hand,” to point by the right hand to the eternal salvation that he seeks. Again it is written: “Your right hand, O Lord, dashes the enemy in pieces” (Ex 15:6), for the enemy, though flourishing in God’s left hand, is shattered in His right hand, because the wicked are often exalted in the present life, but the coming of the eternal blessings (on the great day of the Lord) condemns them.

3.10.11.en: In the Septuagint it reads, “her tongue carries law and mercy,” and St. Augustine comments on this phrase, saying:

3.10.12.en: * Thus concerning the wisdom (of God) it is said: “her tongue carries law and mercy.” The Law that condemns the proud, and the mercy that justifies the humble.

3.10.13.en: * We do not nullify the Law through faith, but we establish it (Rom 3:3), for fear leads to faith. Thus surely the Law brings about wrath, so that God’s mercies may give grace to the sinner, who is terrified and turns to the fulfillment of the righteousness of the Law through Jesus Christ our Lord, who is the wisdom of God of whom it was said: “her tongue carries law and mercy.”

3.10.14.en: By the Law she frightens, and by mercy she helps.

3.10.15.en: The Law was given through His servants, but mercy He offers Himself.

3.10.16.en: The Law was like the staff of Elisha (2 Kgs 4:29 etc.) sent to raise the widow’s son, and it failed to raise him. “For if there had been a law given which could have given life, verily righteousness should have been by the law” (Gal 3:21). But mercy was like Elisha himself, who bore the type of Christ; and by his giving life to the dead he was linked to a great mystery, as with the New Testament.

3.10.17.en: * When it is said: “Let us love one another,” this is law! And when it is said: “For love is of God,” this is grace!

3.10.18.en: For the tongue of the wisdom of God carries law and mercy. Therefore it is said in the Psalm: “He who gives the Law also gives blessings” (cf. Ps 84:6).

3.11.0.en: St. Augustine — “Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace” [17].

3.11.1.en: Wisdom is not only a treasure, which we acquire by acquiring the Creator of treasures, but she also bears a kind of fatherhood or parenthood: she carries believers like little children, that they may lean upon her breast, and she walks with them on the royal way, where believers enjoy heavenly blessings and surpassing peace.

3.12.0.en: She is a tree of life to those who lay hold upon her, and blessed is the one who holds her fast” [18].

3.12.1.en: Thus Wisdom invites us to climb upon her as a tree of life, from which the fruits of the Spirit are plucked, and so we practice the blessed life.

3.12.2.en: If wisdom is a tree of life, then the lazy and the slack will not enjoy her fruit. She is a free divine gift offered to the soul that longs to enjoy her and strives to obtain her. She is the Person of Christ, who desires to offer Himself to us, but by our slackness we deprive ourselves of Him.

3.12.3.en: * Some affirm that the prophet Isaiah referred to these days of the tree of life as the present time of the Church of Christ, and that it was foretold of Christ Himself that He is the tree of life, because He is Wisdom, of whom Solomon says: “She is a tree of life to all who embrace her.”

3.12.4.en: * Rightly it was said of (Wisdom): “She is a tree of life to those who lay hold upon her.” As there was one tree in the material paradise, so there is another tree in the spiritual paradise. The one gives strength to the senses of the outer man and the other to the inner man.

3.12.5.en: St. Augustine — * The prophet Solomon teaches us what this tree of life is, in his exhortation concerning wisdom. She is a tree of life to all who lay hold upon her and lean upon her. This tree is living, not only living but even more guided by reason, meaning that she yields fruit not randomly nor out of season, but in her season. This tree is planted by the streams of water in the region of the Kingdom of God, that is, surely in Paradise, in the place where the stream springs up and divides into four rivers.

3.12.6.en: St. Hilary of Poitiers — * For the tree of life is the Wisdom born before all. “She is a tree of life to those who lay hold upon her,” as the prophet says, “and he who holds her fast is blessed.” She is a tree planted by the streams of water, “that yields her fruit in her season,” meaning that teaching, love and discernment are offered from her storehouses in due season to those who come to the waters of salvation.

3.12.7.en: He who does not believe in Christ, and does not understand that He is the first foundation and the tree of life, and cannot show God his tabernacle adorned with the best fruits, how can he keep the feast? How can he rejoice? Does he not desire the good fruit of the tree? Let them understand the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, how they become more delighted than the sons of men.

3.12.8.en: Father Methodius — “The Lord by wisdom has founded the earth.

3.13.0.en: By understanding has He established the heavens” [19].

3.13.1.en: * Solomon attributes all the elements of creation to the power of wisdom, and adorns her with many names, for by wisdom, prudence, perception, knowledge, understanding and the like he means the same thing.

3.13.2.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa — * If God is the Source of wisdom and life, and is so called, as it is said in Jeremiah: “They have forsaken Me, the fountain of living waters” (Jer 2:13); and also in the Book of Baruch: “You have forsaken the fountain of wisdom” (Bar 3:12), this requires that life and wisdom are not foreign to the essence of the Fountain, but are proper to Him, and were never non-existent, but always existent. Now the Son is all this, He who says: “I am the life” (Jn 14:6), “I wisdom dwell with prudence.” Is it not an error to say that the Son was not at some time? For this means that the Fountain was at some time dry and void of life and wisdom. What recklessness! For God promises those who fulfill His will that they become like an unfailing fountain, saying by Isaiah the prophet: “And satisfy your soul in drought, and strengthen your bones: and you shall be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters fail not” (Isa 58:11), and although the “Fountain of wisdom” is so called, you insult Him as one barren who does not bear His wisdom?!

3.13.3.en: The teachings (of the Arians) are vain, for the truth bears witness that the Fountain of the wisdom of God is eternal, and if the Fountain is eternal, wisdom must be eternal. For in her all things were created, as David says in the Psalm: “In wisdom have You made them all” (Ps 104:24), and Solomon says: “The Lord by wisdom has founded the earth; by understanding has He established the heavens” [19]. This Wisdom is the Word, “All things were made by Him; and without Him was not any thing made that was made” (Jn 1:3).

3.14.0.en: St. Athanasius the Apostolic — “By His knowledge the depths are broken up, and the clouds drop down the dew” [20].

3.14.1.en: In wisdom He was resolved to cleave the great deeps to bring water to the earth, and by it He established the laws of nature so that the earth might enjoy the dew and the rains.

3.14.2.en: If God cares for the needs of the earth, which He created for man, and gave it the waters of oceans, lakes and rivers, and poured upon it rains from above, how would He not care for man? In His love He gives us, in our depths, waters flowing in the heart like rivers of living water, which turn the dryness and wilderness of the heart into the fruitful paradise of God. He also rains upon the heart the dew and showers of the Spirit, that the heart may enjoy all sweetness and rest.

3.15.0.en: 21 My son, let not them depart from your eyes: keep counsel and discretion: 22 So shall they be life unto your soul, and grace to your neck. 23 Then shall you walk in your way safely, and your foot shall not stumble. 24 When you lie down, you shall not be afraid: yes, you shall lie down, and your sleep shall be sweet. 25 Be not afraid of sudden fear, neither of the desolation of the wicked, when it comes. 26 For the Lord shall be your confidence, and shall keep your foot from being taken.

3.15.1.en: If God cleaves in our depths rivers overflowing with sweet water, and rains upon us with the grace of the Spirit, He warns us against pride and against not seeking counsel, saying:

3.15.2.en: “My son, let not them depart from your eyes.

3.15.4.en: So shall they be life unto your soul, and grace to your neck.

3.15.5.en: Then shall you walk in your way safely, and your foot shall not stumble.

3.15.6.en: When you lie down, you shall not be afraid: yes, you shall lie down, and your sleep shall be sweet.

3.15.7.en: Be not afraid of sudden fear, neither of the desolation of the wicked, when it comes.

3.15.8.en: For the Lord shall be your confidence, and shall keep your foot from being taken” [21-26].

3.15.9.en: The words “let not depart” are repeated in this book (Prov 3:21; 4:21), and they mean the abiding of wisdom within the heart so that it does not turn aside from the truth, but the heart sails like a ship in the course of the royal way. St. Clement of Alexandria used this expression in his speech about women: “Do not wear showy fashions lest you slip away from the truth.”

3.15.10.en: When the believer sets the Lord’s commandment and His wisdom before his eyes, trusting in the riches of His free grace, and seeks a spiritual guidance for his life in the Lord, he walks in the safe way, enjoying the following blessings:

3.15.11.en: · The life of the soul, so that it is not dead and without feeling.

3.15.12.en: · Honor in the eyes of God, where he becomes the object of His delight.

3.15.13.en: · He walks in safety despite the enemy’s opposition to him, for with the bronze feet of Christ (Rev 1:15) he tramples down every opposing stone.

3.15.14.en: · He does not fear the anxieties of the near or distant future, for he knows that his life is in the hands of a loving, wise and almighty God, and that every moment of his life is regulated by the hand of his heavenly Father.

3.15.15.en: · When he lies down he enjoys deep sleep, not the sleep of laziness and slackness, but the sleep of trust and assurance in God’s work with him. He knows that God cares for him even in his dreams, and he finds them heavenly and sweet. Many, when they sleep, fear that they will not wake, but the true believer sleeps assured that if he wakes and finds himself in the presence of the Lord he will sing: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready.” And if he wakes to find himself in this world, he glorifies God in everything.

3.16.0.en: 27 Withhold not good from those to whom it is due, when it is in the power of your hand to do it. 28 Say not unto your neighbor, Go, and come again, and tomorrow I will give; when you have it by you. 29 Devise not evil against your neighbor, seeing he dwells securely by you. 30 Strive not with a man without cause, if he has done you no harm.

3.16.1.en: “Withhold not good from those to whom it is due, when it is in the power of your hand to do it” [27].

3.16.2.en: What does he mean by “those to whom it is due”? Not everything we have is ours, but the needy have a share in what is in our hands. When you give it to them, you have only given them their right, of which we were merely guardians. We are stewards over what belongs to the poor; when we give them what is theirs we are counted faithful stewards, with no merit to us except in the faithfulness we practice by the grace of God.

3.17.0.en: “Say not unto your neighbor, Go, and come again, and tomorrow I will give; when you have it by you” [28].

3.17.1.en: Since the time is short and evil, let us hasten to do good to those who ask for it, lest death come upon us or upon them and we lose our opportunity to enjoy doing good with them.

3.17.2.en: “Devise not evil against your neighbor, seeing he dwells securely by you.

3.18.0.en: Strive not with a man without cause, if he has done you no harm” [29-30].

3.18.1.en: He asks us not to bear a spirit of quarrel and strife, for just as some bear a spirit of love to embrace everyone if possible, others bear a spirit of quarrel and find their pleasure in strife with many.

3.18.2.en: According to the Law it is fitting for us to treat others on a sound basis, so that we do not wrong them, but in the era of grace we rise to treat them as God treats us.

3.19.0.en: 31 Envy not the oppressor, and choose none of his ways. 32 For the perverse is an abomination to the Lord: but His secret is with the upright. 33 The curse of the Lord is in the house of the wicked: but He blesses the habitation of the just. 34 Surely He scorns the scorners: but He gives grace to the humble. 35 The wise shall inherit glory: but fools bear dishonor.

3.19.1.en: “Envy not the oppressor, and choose none of his ways.

3.19.2.en: For the perverse is an abomination to the Lord.

3.19.3.en: But His secret is with the upright” [31-32].

3.19.4.en: It is fitting for us not to envy the oppressor nor imitate him, because by this we become an abomination in the eyes of the Lord. But he who walks uprightly finds in God a friend who speaks with him even about His surpassing divine secrets.

3.19.5.en: Truly, many throughout the ages envy the rich even if they are oppressors, but in the end they discover that God condemns the wicked rich, as the psalmist says (Ps 37).

3.19.6.en: Asaph almost slipped away from the faith, because he envied the wicked their success. “For I was envious of the proud, when I saw the peace of the wicked, for there are no pangs in their death, and their body is fat; they are not in the toil of men, and with men they are not afflicted” (Ps 73:3-5). But when he drew near to the sanctuaries of God, and looked to the end of their life, he realized “how they became a desolation suddenly” (Ps 73:19). He cried out: “Whom have I in heaven but You? And with You I desire nothing upon earth” (Ps 73:25), and he ended his psalm with the words: “But it is good for me to draw near to God: I have put my refuge in the Lord God, that I may declare all Your works” (Ps 73:28).

3.19.7.en: Though the oppressor obtains many temporal blessings, he bears an abomination before the Lord, while the righteous or upright in heart comes to know the surpassing mysteries of God.

3.19.8.en: “The curse of the Lord is in the house of the wicked: but He blesses the habitation of the just.

3.19.9.en: Surely He scorns the scorners: but He gives grace to the humble.

3.20.0.en: The wise shall inherit glory: but fools bear dishonor” [33-35].

3.20.1.en: With God there is no curse, but He is the source of every blessing. But the wicked person, determined on evil, since he insists on being estranged from God, deprives himself by his own will of the source of blessings, and so falls into the curse, which takes place with divine permission as the fruit of the evil work. Therefore it is figuratively called “the curse of the Lord.”

3.20.2.en: * As it is written: “God resists the proud, and gives grace to the humble” (Prov 3:34; 1 Pet 5:5; Jas 4:6). Now this grace is a gift from God. But the greatest of gifts is the Holy Spirit Himself, and so He was called “grace.”
